ambiguities: The content of exercise 2.5.41 is unavailable, so its normality conclusion cannot be checked from the supplied proof.
The proof invokes the nonabelian hypothesis without explicitly introducing arbitrary nonabelian groups or proving that the selected elements generate them.
The intended ranges of the exponents $i,j$ in the normal-form argument are unspecified.
“1-to-l” is presumably a typographical error for “1-to-1.”
The proof does not explicitly explain how replacing an order-3 generator by its inverse interchanges conjugation exponents 2 and 4, which is needed to cover arbitrary pairs of groups.

nodes.claim: Cauchy's theorem supplies elements of orders 3 and 7 because both primes divide 21.
nodes.text:
\begin{proof}

    By Cauchy's theorem we have that if $G$ is a group of order 21 then it has an element $a$ of order 3 and an element $b$ of order 7.

nodes.claim: The cited exercise is used to assert that $\langle b\rangle$ is normal; normality then implies $aba^{-1}=b^i$ for some residue $i$ modulo 7. The cited result is not supplied.
nodes.text: By exercise 2.5.41 we have that the subgroup generated by $b$ is normal, so there is some $i=0,1,2,3,4,5,6$ such that $a b a^{-1}=b^i$.

nodes.claim: The argument correctly excludes $i=0$. Excluding $i=1$ requires the unstated fact that $a$ and $b$ generate $G$; this follows from a subgroup-order argument using normality, but that argument is omitted.
nodes.text: We know $i \neq$ 0 since that implies $a b=a$ and so that $b=e$, a contradiction, and we know $i \neq 1$ since then $a b=b a$ and this would imply $G$ is abelian, which we are assuming is not the case.

nodes.claim: Iterating conjugation three times gives $a^3ba^{-3}=b^{i^3}$; since $a^3=e$ and $b$ has order 7, this yields $i^3\equiv1\pmod 7$.
nodes.text: Now, $a$ has order 3 so we must have $b=a^3 b a^{-3}=b^{i^3}$ mod 7 , and so $i$ is restricted by the modular equation $i^3 \equiv 1 \bmod 7$

nodes.claim: The table correctly computes the cubes modulo 7 for residues 2 through 6.
Among residues modulo 7 satisfying $i^3\equiv1$, the possibilities are 1, 2, and 4; the preceding nonabelian argument is intended to exclude 1.
nodes.text: Therefore the only options are $i=2$ and $i=4$.

nodes.claim: This introduces the special case in which the conjugation exponents for $G$ and $G'$ are respectively 2 and 4.
nodes.text: Now suppose $G$ is such that $a b a^{-1}=b^2$ and let $G^{\prime}$ be another group of order 21 with an element $c$ of order 3 and an element $d$ of order 7 such that $c d c^{-1}=d^4$.

nodes.claim: Images are assigned to the proposed generators, but equality of their orders does not establish that the assignment extends to a well-defined function or homomorphism; generation and preservation of all defining relations are needed.
nodes.text:
We now prove that $G$ and $G^{\prime}$ are isomorphic. Define

$$

\begin{aligned}

\phi: G & \rightarrow G^{\prime} \\

a & \mapsto c^{-1} \\

b & \mapsto d

\end{aligned}

$$

since $a$ and $c^{-1}$ have the same order and $b$ and $d$ have the same order this is a well defined function.

nodes.claim: The calculation is invalid: $(cd^{-1}c^{-1})^{-1}=cdc^{-1}$, not $c^{-1}dc$, and $\phi(b)^2=d^2$, not $d^4$. Consequently this node does not establish that $\phi$ is a homomorphism.
nodes.text:
Since

$$

\begin{aligned}

\phi(a) \phi(b) \phi(a)^{-1} & =c^{-1} d c \\

& =\left(c d^{-1} c^{-1}\right)^{-1} \\

& =\left(d^{-4}\right)^{-1} \\

& =d^4 \\

& =\left(d^2\right)^2 \\

& =\phi(b)^2

\end{aligned}

$$

$\phi$ is actually a homomorphism.

nodes.claim: Surjectivity and injectivity are asserted, but the proof has not established a homomorphism or unique normal forms. The assertion that only $i=j=0$ works is false for unrestricted integer exponents and requires specified residue ranges.
nodes.text: For any $c^i d^j \in G^{\prime}$ we have $\phi\left(a^{-i} b^j\right)=c^i d^j$ so $\phi$ is onto and $\phi\left(a^i b^j\right)=c^{-i} d^j=e$ only if $i=j=0$, so $\phi$ is 1-to-l.

nodes.claim: The claimed isomorphism and uniqueness conclusion do not follow from the supplied argument because well-definedness, homomorphism, surjectivity, and injectivity remain unproved, and arbitrary pairs have not explicitly been reduced to the selected exponent cases.
nodes.text:
Therefore $G$ and $G^{\prime}$ are isomorphic and so up to isomorphism there is only one nonabelian group of order 21 .

\end{proof}
